name: Islamic Cairo in one day: how the city grew
note: Orientation: Fustat (641), al-Qata'i (Ibn Tulun 870), Fatimid al-Qahira (969, walled city between Bab al-Futuh and Bab Zuwayla), Saladin's Citadel (1176), Mamluk golden age (1250-1517), Ottoman, Muhammad Ali. UNESCO site. The route: Khan el-Khalili, al-Muizz, then Sultan Hassan, Citadel, Abdeen.

name: Fatimids, Ayyubids, Mamluks, Ottomans: a 5-minute cheat sheet
note: Fatimids: Shia caliphs from Tunisia, founded al-Qahira 'the Victorious' 969, al-Azhar. Ayyubids: Saladin (Kurdish), Sunni restoration, Citadel. Mamluks: slave-soldiers who became sultans, defeated Mongols at Ain Jalut 1260, built most of what you see (Qalawun, al-Nasir, Hassan, Barquq, Qaytbay, al-Ghuri). Ottomans 1517. Muhammad Ali 1805 and his dynasty to Farouk 1952. How to tell styles apart: striped ablaq, muqarnas, stone domes with carved patterns.

name: Khan el-Khalili
note: Built 1382 by emir Jaharkas al-Khalili over the Fatimid caliphs' tombs (he threw out the bones); rebuilt by Sultan al-Ghuri c. 1511 (the surviving gates); the lanes by trade (goldsmiths, coppersmiths, spices, perfume); al-Fishawi café (since 1773) and Naguib Mahfouz; bargaining culture; the Muski street; what is real vs made in China.

name: El Fishawi café and Naguib Mahfouz
note: Short. Open 24h since 1773, mirrors and brass; Nobel laureate Mahfouz wrote there; mint tea, sahlab, shisha; expect tissue sellers and oud players; the Mahfouz novels set in these alleys (Midaq Alley, Cairo Trilogy).

name: Al-Azhar Mosque and University
note: Founded 970-972 by the Fatimids as a Shia foundation, became the chief Sunni university after Saladin; five minarets from different centuries (Qaytbay's double-finial, al-Ghuri's); the Fatimid courtyard; students from all over the Muslim world; dress and shoe etiquette; Sheikh al-Azhar's role today.

name: Al-Hussein Mosque
note: Said to hold the head of Hussein, the Prophet's grandson, brought from Ascalon in 1153; Cairo's most beloved shrine, the mawlid crowds; the 1870s Ottoman-Gothic rebuild; non-Muslims may not be admitted inside the shrine; the square's cafés.

name: Al-Muizz Street: the Fatimid spine
note: 1 km from Bab al-Futuh to Bab Zuwayla along the Fatimid Qasaba, 'the greatest concentration of medieval monuments in the Islamic world'; Bayn al-Qasrayn 'between the two palaces' where the Fatimid palaces stood; restored 2008, pedestrian; order of monuments walking south; Mahfouz's Palace Walk; lit at night.

name: Bab al-Futuh and Bab al-Nasr, the Fatimid gates
note: Built 1087 by Armenian vizier Badr al-Jamali with three architects from Edessa; Byzantine-style military architecture, rounded (Futuh) vs square (Nasr) towers, machicolations; Napoleon's troops carved their names (Tour Julien); the wall walk between them; the Northern Cemetery beyond.

name: Mosque of al-Hakim
note: Begun 990, finished 1013 by the 'mad caliph' al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah who banned molokheya and women's shoes, vanished on the Muqattam in 1021 (Druze await his return); the odd minaret bastions; used as a prison for Crusaders, Napoleon's fort, a boys' school; rebuilt in marble by the Bohra Ismailis 1980.

name: Bayt al-Suhaymi: a Cairene merchant's house
note: 1648 + 1796, Darb al-Asfar; the salamlik/haramlik split, mashrabiya screens (see out, not in, cool the air, jars of water), the courtyard garden, the bath, the marble fountains in the qa'a; how wealthy Ottoman Cairo lived; Mahfouz's Palace Walk house.

name: Sabil-Kuttab of Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda
note: 1744, where the street forks: a sabil (public fountain, charity water from a cistern) below and a kuttab (Quran school for orphans) above; Iznik-style tiles inside; the type is Cairo's signature charity building; Katkhuda the great Ottoman patron.

name: Al-Aqmar Mosque: the 'moonlit' façade
note: 1125, first Cairo mosque with a decorated stone street façade aligned to the street while the interior turns to Mecca; the shell niche with 'Muhammad' and 'Ali' medallion (Shia Fatimid); the 'bent' plan; tiny and easy to miss.

name: Complex of Sultan Qalawun: mausoleum, madrasa and hospital
note: 1284-85, built in 13 months with Crusader columns from Acre; the mausoleum is the most lavish Mamluk interior in Cairo (marble, mother-of-pearl, stucco, the dome's inner octagon echoing the Dome of the Rock); the bimaristan hospital treated all free with music therapy and separate wards, operated 600 years; the madrasa; Qalawun founder of a dynasty.

name: Madrasa of al-Nasir Muhammad (with the Gothic portal)
note: 1295-1304; the marble Gothic portal was looted from a Crusader church in Acre (1291) and re-erected here, a trophy; the stucco minaret with North African/Andalusian style; al-Nasir Muhammad's three reigns and Cairo's peak.

name: Madrasa-Khanqah of Sultan Barquq
note: 1384-86, first Circassian (Burji) Mamluk sultan; the bronze-plated door, porphyry columns, the painted ceiling of the prayer hall; the Sufi khanqah function; Barquq's daughter buried in the dome, he himself in the Northern Cemetery.

name: Al-Ghuri complex and Wikala: the last Mamluk sultan
note: 1503-05, mosque-madrasa and mausoleum facing each other across the street (the roof once covered the silk market); Qansuh al-Ghuri died at Marj Dabiq 1516 fighting the Ottomans, body never found; the Wikala al-Ghuri caravanserai (five storeys, merchants below, lodgings above) now hosts the Tannoura Sufi whirling show (Wed/Sat evenings).

name: Mosque of Sultan al-Mu'ayyad and Bab Zuwayla
note: The 1092 southern Fatimid gate where heads were displayed and the last Mamluk sultan Tumanbay was hanged by the Ottomans in 1517 (rope broke twice); al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh built his mosque 1415-21 on the site of the prison where he had been held, and put his twin minarets on top of the gate: climb them for the best view of the street; the door was taken from Sultan Hassan's mosque.

name: Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Hassan
note: 1356-63, built with Black Death inheritances; 36 m portal, the four iwans for the four Sunni law schools with student cells behind; the cruciform plan, the chains of lamps, the mausoleum behind the qibla (Hassan's body never found, two sons buried there); the minaret that collapsed killing 300; used as a fortress to bombard the Citadel; scale: 150 m long, 8,000 m2.

name: Al-Rifa'i Mosque: royal tombs and the Shah of Iran
note: 1869-1912, commissioned by Khedive Ismail's mother Khushyar Hanim to mirror Sultan Hassan across the street; neo-Mamluk; tombs of Khedive Ismail, King Fuad I, King Farouk (died Rome 1965) and the last Shah of Iran Mohammad Reza Pahlavi (1980) whose first wife Fawzia was Farouk's sister; Sufi sheikh al-Rifa'i's shrine.

name: The Citadel of Saladin
note: Begun 1176 by Saladin with Crusader prisoners and stones from small Giza pyramids; seat of government for 700 years until Khedive Ismail moved to Abdeen 1874; Muhammad Ali's 1811 massacre of the Mamluks at the Bab al-Azab gate (the legend of the one who jumped his horse over the wall); Northern vs Southern enclosures; what to see in 90 minutes; the view over Cairo to the pyramids on a clear day.

name: Mosque of Muhammad Ali (the Alabaster Mosque)
aliases: big Ottoman mosque on the Citadel
note: 1830-48 by Yusuf Bushnaq, an Istanbul-style Ottoman mosque (like Sultan Ahmed) deliberately un-Mamluk to mark the new dynasty; alabaster cladding from Beni Suef; the clock tower a 1845 gift from Louis-Philippe in exchange for the Luxor obelisk (now in Paris), reportedly never worked; Muhammad Ali's tomb (moved 1857); the chandeliers and the 365 lamps.

name: Mosque of al-Nasir Muhammad on the Citadel
note: 1318-35, the only Mamluk building left on the Citadel, royal mosque of the sultans; reused Pharaonic and Roman columns in the arcades; the two minarets with Persian-style green faience tops (Tabriz craftsmen); the Ottomans used it as a stable; the Selim I Ottoman conquest.

name: Gawhara Palace and the Mamluk massacre site
note: Short. 1814 palace of Muhammad Ali (named after his last wife Gawhara), French-Ottoman style, where he received envoys; his portrait, the throne; fire in 1972; near the Bab al-Azab where the 470 Mamluk beys were shot in 1811 after a banquet.

name: Joseph's Well (Bir Yusuf)
note: Short. 87 m spiral well cut through rock by Crusader prisoners c. 1176 to give the Citadel water in a siege; oxen walked down the ramp to turn the waterwheels; named after Saladin (Yusuf), not the biblical Joseph; usually closed, viewable from above.

name: The Egyptian Military Museum (Harim Palace)
note: Short. In Muhammad Ali's Harim Palace (1827); dioramas from Pharaonic armies to 1973; the Korean-made panoramas; mainly for the palace interiors; the tanks outside; skip if short on time.

name: Abdeen Palace
note: Built 1863-74 by Khedive Ismail to move government from the Citadel and make Cairo 'Paris on the Nile'; 500 rooms; the 1942 Abdeen incident when British tanks forced King Farouk to appoint a prime minister; the 1952 revolution; museums open to visitors: arms, royal family, silver, presidential gifts; still a presidential palace: strict security, no photos in parts.

name: Mosque of Ibn Tulun (if you have time)
note: 876-879, Cairo's oldest mosque in original form, Samarra-style brick with the spiral minaret (legend: Ibn Tulun twisted a piece of parchment); 2 km from the Citadel, Gayer-Anderson house next door (Bond's 'The Spy Who Loved Me' scene). Optional detour.

name: How to read a Mamluk building: ablaq, muqarnas, mashrabiya
note: Visual glossary: ablaq striped masonry, muqarnas stalactite vaults over portals, mashrabiya turned-wood screens, iwan vaulted hall, qibla/mihrab/minbar, dikka, sabil, kuttab, madrasa, khanqah, wikala, carved stone domes (zigzag, star), the tiraz inscription band; and the Mamluk blazons (cup for cupbearer, pen box for secretary).
